game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。

Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Oh man this was bad..
If you came here like me, looking for a modern kudos for the dire dystopian worlds of Animal Farm, 1984 etc., don't.

So in the game you basically just comb through whole lot of material and all the relevant parts pop out highlighted and then you drag them into files. You don't even need to read any of it; it's all chewed up for you. You have no say on the content of the data you feed into the system, nor how it is interpreted. You cannot correct wrong conclusions nor any way communicate with the low IQ bully guy making anemic remarks on every data bit you collect. There's hardly any choice for you at all.

Your start the game by researching a woman named Cassandra, and the first thing you get to read is her social media feed. Apparently Cassandra here went to a punk concert and got so excited of it she dyed her hair blue and posted about it online. Her shocked "nice and normal" best friend scolds her for going to a stylist alone and "ruining her beautiful hair", other people cheer on her "becoming punk" and a pierced rocker dude with spiked hair comments "good, now I can finally invite you to our (activist) group". ...Wait, what??

The writing is extremely naive, dumb and ridden with awkward narrow minded stereotypes. I'm dying in agony. It seems like written by very young inexperienced people with not a whole lot of grasp of the world. The game is about you simply chasing down actual criminals from suspects and there is no moral dilemma, no underlying unjust conflict, weird scary social constructs with thought policing nor anything of the likes. It doesn't make you think.

Considering this game is blatantly riding on the great name of Orwell, of all things, it is particularly disastrous. 
It should not have been made. I'm sorry, Mr. George Orwell.

review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the core concept is interesting, the game play and plot leave much to be desired. It is also incredibly short. The TLDR is that I would not recommend this unless the concept really grabs you.

The story revolves around a bombing and the activist group linked to it. You take the role of an investigator using social media, private messages/files and recorded phone calls to get to the bottom of everything. There seem to be a few possible different outcomes which could be interesting to explore if the people involved weren't so... stupid. I wont spoil anything but they basically make their own problems and then make bigger problems for themselves because they incorrectly think the bigger problems will solve their problems. It's like watching a train wreck in slow motion. It can be hard to get invested when you can't relate or empathise with the characters. I found myself thinking that most of them were horrible people who deserved what the plot threw at them.

The game play consists of reading through documents and chat logs and dragging over information that you determine to be relevant to the case. Some of this information is incorrect or contradictory and so you must vet information before committing it to the system. There are no taking information back even if you find contradicting information later on. This means a lot of your time will be spent going back and forward between different documents to pick out information and drag it to the appropriate file. This isn't exactly the most invigorating game play but when you are in the zone it can be somewhat enjoyable.

There isn't really much else to say. The game does have a political agenda and a underlying moral to it but it kind of falls on its face to the extent that I started to wonder if the resistant reading was the intended one.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Spying on citizens of a (not-so) future dystopian society in an attempt to convict them of crimes and uncover some deeper conspiracy sounds good on paper, but does not work so well in game form; at least not if it is done like Orwell does it. For 5 hours, you read through text, sort datachunks to their respective profiles, and read unskippable text / call exchanges between the subjects. That is pretty much it. The story is a bit slow and does only gain steam in the last two episodes 4 and 5, but the "gameplay" remains the same.

Perhaps even more annoying is that there is no overall lesson to be learned here; it is very much a self-containing story with no real moral aside from the obvious and ham-fisted "government can see everything you do = bad", which does not even really stick the landing as the game actually shows a few reasons for why the government may want to do such a thing, right or not.

As a game, there is not much here aside from essentially reading a more tedious novel while constantly having to switch between profiles with little choice until the end. As a story, there is some good here, but it is not engaging enough even despite the short length.

Short game with an interesting concept; that, in my opinion, failed to deliver. For the most part, the game does a good job keeping you guessing if you are making the right choices; but overall, I found the game boring and kept playing only to finish the story, just to be disappointed.

The story was interesting enough to keep me playing. You are an investigator working for a government surveillance system trying to unravel a terrorist group. The game wants you to deal with all the moral struggle that comes with invading people's privacy, but I think the premise falls flat. There were many times throughout the game where I felt it was finally about to get good, but it never materialized. Then the last chapter throws everything overboard: [spoiler] the criminal out themselves undermining all the mystery; the game tries to guilt you into feeling bad for people who had done terrible things; and, for some reason, you are supposed to side with them in the end. [/spoiler]

Too many conflicted opinions to recommend this one. I believe there is a Demo; try it first.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]:

review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

At first comment, this is much more a novel / interactive story than a game.

On playthrough, not a good "game". Only 1 "story" which you are forced into watching, and no sandbox. Only big red buttons to click to reveal info that progress the story. No side missions, or broadness.

Quite well presented, but very, very thin. Worth £1-2.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Painfully linear story telling. The choices in the game aren't really moral dilemmas on your part, it's a matter of trying to guess if the vague phrasing about a character's behavior is intentionally loaded with meaning or just bad writing within the game. There is almost zero re-play value and while it is 'pretty' it's very limited in terms of choices and interactive activity. If the game doesn't want you clicking on a certain item, it just sends you through a series of loops of graphics, which can also be confusing at the start of the game when you're trying to figure out what matters and what will change throughout the 'day' in the investigation. The interface, while accurate, really does remind you of your work computer. That's... not a compliment.

Some of the interesting questions this game briefly poses never get answered - including fleshing out details of certain characters you have compromising information on. In reality, you're not engaging with 90% of the text it tries to force-feed you. You're just searching for highlighted blurbs to obediently click and pass to the next marker. It's disappointing because it could have been so much more.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

"Are they really terrorists?" the game's description asks. And the answer is no. I could have guessed that from the bugged out clip following her getting on a bus that only played the second time I started a new game because the first one I hit a dead end and had no choice but to just start adding data at random hoping something would trigger only to have to google and find out it was a known bug and I just had to restart from the start. So thanks, I hate it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I do not recommend this game. Here's why.
First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse. And then browse and click a bit more. When I want to read (and I love reading) I read books, not games.
Second thing - visuals. Yes, the game's style and interface are aesthetically pleasing. But... first developers show lack of any effort to make the game rich in gameplay, then do the same with graphics. Yes they use nice colors. Yes the font is elegant. But it's easy to see how it was designed to be made quickly and effortlessly with those simple vectors. Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas.
And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there was a "Maybe" rating. This was so solidly middle of the road. A Perfect 2.5/5. This game is a narrative uncovered through a government surveillance system, and we're really taking the good with the bad here. 

The good: The mechanics of the game are interesting, and pay off in a very satisfying way. The visuals are nice and the interface is inoffensive. 

The bad: The character writing is mealymouthed, badly-paced and lacking a fresh core message. The narrative is hung on characters that are one-dimensional. The message is nothing new, but the 1984 But It's Got Facebook appeal could sell it's rhetorical points a lot easier if these characters felt rounder or even spoke in a slightly modern voice. A game where you follow people's daily communications should lead to these characters feeling richer and more developed. To it's credit, the story itself had some really interesting and surprising turns! But it was all at the end, AND all at once in a truly maddening choice of pacing.

All this is... fine, I suppose, considering these characters' actions and moral codas don't feel meaningfully attached to the larger ethical decision you're ultimately faced with. Instead, I felt like I was reading a 90's screenplay about Post-college Anarchist Mallrats and their One Cool Professor trying to make their mark on the world. Mostly because Orwell takes itself really, painfully seriously.

Overall, worth playing for the moments where the story and gameplay align nicely, but DEFINITELY get it on sale. Full price? Idk. Torrent Hackers instead. It has the same self-important tone and fakey computer-whiz stuff, but at least that had Angelina Jolie in it.

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[h1]
 I thought I was going to find something different, something I could replay once and again. I really think the game has a lot of potential, but I can't recommend it.

To be clear, this isn't a BAD game. I really liked the concepts behind it and the story was interesting, albeit a bit short. But I wouldn't recommend the game to other players for the following reason: it doesn't really engross the player in such a way that you feel like part of the story or that your choices matter. Now, I'm SURE the choices you make matter in the sense that which data is submitted ends up controlling some part of the narrative that plays out, but all the while playing this game it felt like there was really little for me to go out and find on my own or decisions for me to make.

Admittedly I probably need to give this another go and try making some different data-submissions to try trigger some alternate script, but ultimately I didn't see enough in this play-thru that makes the juice look worth the squeeze.

FWIW - I did enjoy the music. Really reminiscent of Hacknet.

review_text_raw:
I love the game mechanics!

However, I wish the game gave players more power to decide what actions to take.

Since you’re just an information collector, the only way to influence the outcome is by choosing not to feed certain information to your supervisor. That limits a lot of freedom because you can't really control what a scripted supervisor thinks. And sometimes, if you don’t feed the plot-required information, the game just stops and waits for you, forcing you to still somewhat follow the intended plot. The illusion of "choice matter" in this case is worse than reading a visual novel.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A lightly interactive storytelling presentation where you're the surveillance state, combing through people's files and conversations... but then uh-oh! get this! what if the surveillance state ISN'T A GOOD THING? Gosh! 

"Papers, Please" seems to be the aspiration here. Well, that game manages to pull off something affecting because 1) it has an actual gameplay component that cleverly creates tension with the ethics, and 2) its writing is terse and flavorful and very carefully styled. Orwell is 0 for 2.

Basically, the piece as a whole is exactly as literate and well-considered and native-English-speaking as its title: "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You." If you think that title sounds cool, you might well find this a compelling experience; clearly many people do. But if you're raising an eyebrow at it, I encourage you to just trust your gut and move along.
